newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia renews attack on currency speculators.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia renews attack on currency speculators.

text.p: Malaysia renewed its attack on currency speculators on Monday while U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said Washington was watching developments in Asian financial markets very closely.

In an opening address to a meeting of leading Asian and Western nations, Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi said it was troubling that Southeast Asian economies "continue to be bedevilled by currency fluctuations caused by hostile elements bent on such unholy actions".
He said it was the "height of international criminality" that the fate of millions could be subject to the mercy of a few "unscrupulous" traders.
"We in ASEAN have resolved to intensify actions to take counter-measures. It is time that we recognise these actions for what they really are, namely villainous acts of sabotage," Abdullah said.
Albright in turn told a meeting of the nine members of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) and their 10 so-called dialogue partners of leading Asian and Western powers:
"The United States has been watching developments in Southeast Asian financial markets very closely. Our Treasury Department is in close contact with the IMF (International Monetary Fund)."

Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad has openly accused U.S. billionaire George Soros of leading a speculative assault after the currencies of Thailand, the Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia in particular came under recent attack.
Soros has denied attempts to destabilise Asian currencies.

ASEAN comprises Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore, Indonesia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Brunei, Burma and Laos. The dialogue partners are the United States, Japan, China, Russia, South Korea, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, India and the European Union.

ASEAN held its annual foreign ministers' conference last week, while ministers held political and security discussions with leading Asian and Western powers under the umbrella of the ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF) on Sunday.
On Monday and Tuesday, ASEAN meets the dialogue partners to discuss regional and international issues ranging from economic cooperation to the fight against drugs and terrorism.
Ministers praised the progress ASEAN has made over the past 30 years, including economic cooperation which has boosted the region into one of the world's economic powerhouses.
Albright noted that ASEAN now represented the fourth largest trading partner for the United States, with American investment in the region exceeding $35 billion.

Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda said the region had achieved spectacular development, but he noted increasing constraints on aid from donor nations and said the limited funds available should be used more efficiently and effectively.

Cambodia and international efforts led by ASEAN to broker a settlement to the political crisis there have so far dominated the meetings, which opened with a two-day meeting of the ASEAN foreign ministers last Thursday.

ASEAN Secretary-General Ajit Singh told Reuters on Monday three ASEAN foreign ministers headed by Indonesia's Ali Alatas would go to Phnom Penh as soon as Cambodian strongman Hun Sen had clarified his attitude towards mediation.

Earlier this month, Second Prime Minister Hun Sen rebuffed an ASEAN mediation effort to end the crisis in Cambodia, precipitated when he staged a bloody putsch to oust coalition colleague and First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh.
Western nations led by the United States have also been sharply critical of Burma, although accepting its membership in ASEAN as an accomplished fact after its admittance with Laos last Wednesday.
Albright has called on other ASEAN states to use their influence on Rangoon's military rulers to promote human rights and democracy, and on Monday slammed Burma as a primary source of drugs.
